Here is a parent-facing version in plain language:

---

# Why we are changing how maths is taught

From next year, our school will move from teaching children in “ability sets” for maths to teaching them in **mixed-attainment classes**.

We know some parents may feel unsure about this change. That is understandable. Many people went to school in sets themselves and may feel that this is the best way. We want to explain clearly why we are making this change, and how we will make sure **every child is supported and challenged**.

## What does this change mean?

At the moment, children are often put into different groups based on how well they seem to be doing in maths.

With mixed-attainment teaching, children of different starting points learn together in the same class. This does **not** mean all children do exactly the same work in exactly the same way. Teachers will still:

- give extra support where it is needed
- stretch pupils who are ready for more challenge
- use questioning, practice, and tasks that allow all children to learn and improve

## Why are we making this change?

### 1. Children learn at different speeds
A child’s progress in maths is not fixed. Some children take longer to understand a new idea, then make rapid progress later. Some do well early on but need more help as the work becomes harder.

A set placed at one point in time does not always reflect what a child can achieve in the future.

### 2. High expectations matter
When children are placed in lower sets, they can sometimes be given easier work for too long. This can limit confidence and progress.

In mixed-attainment classes, all pupils are taught important maths ideas and are given the chance to think, reason, and solve problems. We want every child to have access to a rich maths education.

### 3. Children benefit from learning with others
Talking about maths helps children learn. When pupils explain their thinking, listen to different ideas, and solve problems together, their understanding becomes stronger.

This benefits children at all levels. Explaining an idea helps deepen understanding, and hearing another pupil explain something in a new way can make it clearer.

### 4. Ability is not fixed
We do not believe that children should be defined too early as “good at maths” or “not good at maths”. Confidence, practice, teaching, and effort all make a difference.

Our aim is for children to see maths as something they can improve at, not something they either have or do not have.

## Will my child still be challenged?

Yes.

A common worry is that children who are already doing well in maths will be held back. We will not allow that to happen.

In mixed-attainment lessons, challenge comes from:
- deeper thinking, not just harder numbers
- explaining and proving answers
- solving more complex problems
- making links between different maths ideas
- extension tasks for pupils who are ready

Children who grasp ideas quickly will be expected to think hard, reason clearly, and go deeper in their understanding.

## Will my child still get help if they struggle?

Yes.

A child who finds maths difficult will not be left behind. Teachers will:
- break learning into small steps
- check understanding carefully
- give extra explanation and practice
- use worked examples and clear routines
- provide support in class
- offer extra help where needed

Mixed-attainment teaching is not about expecting every child to cope alone. It is about making sure all children can take part in strong maths teaching, with the right support.

## Why not keep setting if it seems simpler?

Setting can seem like the easiest answer, but it does not always lead to better learning for all children.

In some cases, children in lower sets can receive a narrower curriculum and have fewer chances to develop confidence. Once placed in a lower group, it can also be hard to move up, even when a child improves.

We want a system that keeps doors open, not one that closes them too early.

## What will good mixed-attainment teaching look like?

Parents should expect to see:
- clear explanations from the teacher
- careful step-by-step teaching
- opportunities for children to talk about maths
- practice to build confidence and fluency
- questions that make children think
- support for those who need it
- challenge for those ready to go further

This change is not about lowering standards. It is about **raising expectations for all pupils**.

## Our commitment to parents

We know that parents want their children to do well, feel confident, and leave school with strong maths skills. We want that too.

We are making this change because we believe it gives more children the chance to succeed, while still supporting and stretching every learner.

We will keep reviewing how the new approach is working and will listen to feedback from parents, pupils, and staff.

If you have questions or worries, please speak to us. We want to work together to help every child succeed in maths.
